title: Pas de Cécile, pas de Paris  (No Cécile, No Paris)

segments.t: Mathias is still negotiating with Miranda, the film producer who turned Cecile down. When she asks about permits to shoot in Paris, he sees a way to reopen the casting decision. Listen to the French conversation first; the main idea matters more than every word.
Vous avez les autorisations pour tourner à Paris?
Ah, la paperasse française!
Oui, c'est difficile.
C'est plus simple quand on connaît les bonnes personnes.
Vraiment?
Si vous avez besoin d'aide, demandez.
Je connais la ministre de la Culture. C'est une jeune femme brillante.
Et elle adore Cécile de France!
Mais Cécile n'est plus dans le projet.
Je sais. Elle va être très triste.
Alors, tourner à Paris, c'est peut-être impossible.
Elle n'a pas besoin de le savoir.
Elles sont très proches. C'est difficile de cacher la vérité.
Vous bluffez.
Pas du tout. Pas de Cécile, pas de Paris.
Let's take it slowly. Miranda opens with what she wants, and the verb she uses is the film-world word for shooting a scene.
Vous avez les autorisations pour tourner à Paris?
'Do you have the permits to shoot in Paris?' Mathias puts the polite 'you' before 'have'. The action at the end means making a film, rather than turning an object.
Ah, la paperasse française!
'Ah, French paperwork!' The description 'French' takes a feminine form to match 'paperwork'. Its final consonant becomes audible in this form.
Oui, c'est difficile.
'Yes, it's difficult.' A short description after 'it's' is enough to agree with Miranda's complaint. Mathias then offers a way around the problem.
C'est plus simple quand on connaît les bonnes personnes.
'It's simpler when you know the right people.' The word in the middle means 'one' or 'people in general'. It sounds like a hint, and it is one.
Vraiment?
'Really?' Miranda is curious now. One word, rising at the end.
Si vous avez besoin d'aide, demandez.
'If you need help, just ask.' Notice the polite form of 'you' all through this scene: Mathias and Miranda are business partners, so they stay formal. The last word is a polite command, 'ask'.
Je connais la ministre de la Culture.
'I know the Minister of Culture.' The action word means to know a person. And the minister is a woman, so she gets the feminine 'the'.
C'est une jeune femme brillante.

'She's a brilliant young woman.' In this phrase 'young' goes before the noun and 'brilliant' after it. Adjective position is something to learn with the particular description, rather than from its length.
Et elle adore Cécile de France!
'And she loves Cécile de France!' The action word is stronger than just 'like': it means 'adore'. Miranda sees the problem coming.
Mais Cécile n'est plus dans le projet.

'But Cécile isn't in the project any more.' Here is our second language point. The negative in French wraps around the action word, and when the second half is this word, it means 'no longer', 'not any more'.
Je sais. Elle va être très triste.
'I know. She's going to be very sad.' To talk about the near future, take the verb 'to go' and add an infinitive, exactly like 'going to be' in English.
Alors, tourner à Paris, c'est peut-être impossible.
'So shooting in Paris might be impossible.' The small hyphenated expression means 'perhaps'. Mathias uses uncertainty to make his threat sound indirect.
Elle n'a pas besoin de le savoir.
'She doesn't need to know.' The negative wraps around the verb again, this time with the ordinary 'not'. Mathias doesn't let go.
Elles sont très proches.
'They're very close.' The pronoun here is the plural for women, since both are women: the minister and Cécile.
C'est difficile de cacher la vérité.
'It's hard to hide the truth.' After the description 'difficult', a short linking word introduces the action. Notice that 'truth' has a definite article, as in English here.
Vous bluffez.
'You're bluffing.' The same word as in poker, with the polite form of 'you'. And now the line of the scene.
Pas du tout.
'Not at all.' This three-word reply strengthens the refusal. You can use it on its own when denying an accusation, as Mathias does here.
Pas de Cécile, pas de Paris.

'No Cecile, no Paris.' Without a verb, the negative word pairs with a short link to each name. The tea-room conversation ends with that threat; outside, Mathias confirms to another man that this is a rescue operation. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more.
Vous avez les autorisations pour tourner à Paris?
Ah, la paperasse française!
Oui, c'est difficile.
C'est plus simple quand on connaît les bonnes personnes.
Vraiment?
Si vous avez besoin d'aide, demandez.
Je connais la ministre de la Culture. C'est une jeune femme brillante.
Et elle adore Cécile de France!
Mais Cécile n'est plus dans le projet.
Je sais. Elle va être très triste.
Alors, tourner à Paris, c'est peut-être impossible.
Elle n'a pas besoin de le savoir.
Elles sont très proches. C'est difficile de cacher la vérité.
Vous bluffez.
Pas du tout. Pas de Cécile, pas de Paris.
That's the end of this scene. When you watch it, listen for the short, punchy line about Cécile and Paris; you'll recognise it straight away. See you next time!
Au revoir, Mathias!
